scenes.heading: Physical properties of substances
scenes.sub: Why does dry ice skip the liquid?
scenes.say: Why does dry ice turn straight into gas? Why does a pressure cooker cook faster? And why is diamond hard while copper bends? It's a balance between the forces holding particles together and the energy pushing them apart.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: At a party, energy goes into breaking up groups, not moving faster
scenes.science: On a heating-curve plateau, energy separates particles: T stays flat
scenes.breaks: on a real plateau the two phases are in equilibrium, with particles changing phase in both directions.
scenes.say: A heating-curve plateau is like a party breaking up. The extra energy doesn't make anyone move faster. It goes into pulling groups apart. So the temperature stays flat. The boiling plateau is longer, because for water, delta H of vaporisation is forty point seven kilojoules per mole, but delta H of fusion is only six point zero one.
scenes.caption: A heating-curve plateau is like a party breaking up. The extra energy doesn't make anyone move faster. It goes into pulling groups apart, so the temperature stays flat. The boiling plateau is longer: for water, ΔH_vap is 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ but ΔH_fus is only 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹.

scenes.heading: Worked example: heating curve
scenes.question: How much heat turns 25.0 g of ice at −15.0 °C into water at 40.0 °C?
scenes.say: Split it into stages. Sloping parts use q equals m c delta T, and flat parts use q equals n delta H. Warming the ice takes zero point seven eight four kilojoules. Melting takes eight point three four. Warming the water takes four point one eight. The total is thirteen point three kilojoules.
scenes.caption: Split it into stages. Sloping parts use q = mcΔT, and flat parts use q = nΔH. Warming the ice takes 0.784 kJ. Melting takes 8.34 kJ. Warming the water takes 4.18 kJ. The total is 13.3 kJ.

scenes.heading: Boiling is a pressure contest
points: Boils when vapour pressure = outside pressure
Mountain top: lower pressure, boils below 100 °C
Vapour pressure: substance and T only
scenes.say: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the outside pressure. On a mountain, water boils below one hundred degrees. In a pressure cooker, it boils at about one hundred and twenty. Vapour pressure depends only on the substance and temperature.
scenes.caption: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the outside pressure. On a mountain, water boils below 100 °C. In a pressure cooker, it boils at about 120 °C. Vapour pressure depends only on the substance and temperature.

scenes.heading: Clausius–Clapeyron
scenes.say: The Clausius–Clapeyron equation links vapour pressure to temperature. Use delta H of vaporisation in joules per mole, R as eight point three one four, and temperatures in kelvin. For water, it predicts about forty-eight kilopascals at eighty degrees.
scenes.caption: The Clausius–Clapeyron equation links vapour pressure to temperature. Use ΔH_vap in J mol⁻¹, R = 8.314, and T in kelvin. For water, it predicts about 48.2 kPa at 80.0 °C.

scenes.heading: Ionic vs metallic solids

left.title: Ionic: brittle
points: Shift a layer: like charges meet

right.title: Metallic: malleable
points: Cations in a sea of electrons

scenes.say: An ionic crystal is like a grid of fridge magnets. Shift a row by half a step and like charges meet, so it cracks. A metal is like marbles in honey. The cations slide, but the delocalised electrons keep holding them together, so metals bend.

points: Slope: q = mcΔT; plateau: q = nΔH
Boils when vapour pressure = outside pressure
CO₂ triple point is above 1 atm: dry ice sublimes
scenes.say: Quick recap. Slopes warm, plateaus change phase. Boiling is a pressure contest. Water's solid–liquid line slopes backwards because ice floats. And dry ice sublimes because carbon dioxide's triple point is above one atmosphere. Now try the practice questions!
